title: The School by the Well
premise: A fictional Warring States school explores two distinct accounts of moral cultivation. Mencius and Xunzi are not fused into one correct answer or treated as representatives of all Chinese thought.

items.label: Comparison sheet
items.description: Compare the source of concern, the work of practice, and what each account would say when conduct falls short.

items.label: Comparison table
items.description: Mencian emphasis: nurture beginnings of concern. Xunzian emphasis: form conduct through learned practice. Neither says improvement happens without effort.

items.label: Compassion notes
items.description: Concern can appear before calculation. Does it need cultivation to become dependable care?

items.label: Compassion question
items.description: Why feel concern for a child you do not know, before calculating any advantage?

items.label: Counterexample
items.description: Our fictional pupil feels alarm at the well but freezes. Another has no strong feeling yet follows a practised rescue procedure. What does either case tell us about moral cultivation?

items.label: Cultivation reading
items.description: A Xunzian reading: teachers, ritual and deliberate effort form better habits. Good conduct is cultivated, not secured by following every impulse.

items.label: Mencius reading
items.description: A Mencian reading: an incipient concern can be cultivated, like a sprout. A beginning is not finished virtue; practice still matters.

items.label: Mourning commentary
items.description: In the Xunzi tradition, ritual gives grief a shaped expression. This does not claim every person or culture must grieve through the same forms.

items.label: Music example
items.description: A shared musical practice asks each participant to listen and adjust to others.

items.label: Open question
items.description: A feeling can fail to become action; trained conduct can occur without a strong feeling. Which account better explains what these pupils need next?

items.label: Paired readings
items.description: Both accounts require cultivation. They differ over how to understand its beginnings and the role of learned forms.

items.label: Practice record
items.description: A fictional pupil learns to wait, take turns and attend to others through repeated practice—not a claim that manners alone make a person good.

items.label: Question card
items.description: Where might moral concern begin: a feeling already stirring in us, or conduct learned through practice?

items.label: Ritual notes
items.description: Practice can reshape habits rather than merely express whatever impulse arrives first.

items.label: Ritual text
items.description: A Xunzian question: how do taught forms and deliberate practice shape conduct?

items.label: School manuscript
items.description: Two accounts of cultivation, one difficult case. A sudden feeling and a learned action can come apart. The school leaves that tension visible for its next discussion.

items.label: Seminar record
items.description: The question remains open: what must be nurtured, what must be learned, and how would we tell? The comparison is preserved rather than blended into a third doctrine.

items.label: Teacher response
items.description: Our fictional teacher: do not declare a winner from two imagined cases. Ask what would make concern and considerate action more dependable over time.

items.label: Well account
items.description: Imagine suddenly seeing a child about to fall into a well. Mencius asks about the immediate alarm and concern, apart from seeking a reward. Concern is not a guarantee of rescue.

recipes.description: A child near a well invites Mencius’s question about immediate concern, not a literal experiment on a child.
Xunzi’s ritual discussion gives expression to grief within a specific social account; this is not a claim that grief requires a ritual everywhere.

stages.title: The question by the well
stages.speaker: The teacher
stages.motivation: Why might someone feel concern before thinking of a reward? Make a reading of the well story.

area.label: The question by the well

stages.title: In the practice hall
stages.speaker: The second teacher
stages.motivation: Another account asks what deliberate practice and ritual make possible. Prepare a cultivation reading beside the first.

stages.motivation: One pupil feels alarm but freezes; another follows a practised rescue procedure without strong feeling. Preserve the difficult question in a school manuscript. We need not settle it today.

notes: The characters and encounter are fiction; Mencius and Xunzi were not conducting this seminar together.
Risk: document assembly can become a named checklist. This candidate needs a domain reader and human playtest before expansion.

The freezing pupil and trained responder are original hypothetical examples, not examples attributed to Mencius or Xunzi. This comparison is intentionally selective, not a comprehensive account of either thinker.
